web.title: Idempotency Keys Explained: Stop Duplicate API Retries
web.description: An idempotency key makes a retried POST safe: replay the first response for 24h and treat in-flight keys as a third state — the race most APIs miss.
snippets: Removed after at least 24 hours; reusing a pruned key produces a genuinely new request. Parameters are compared. If the same key arrives with different parameters, that’s an error — it means the client made a mistake, not that it retried. But the replay has a boundary. Anything rejected before the endpoint starts running is not covered. Rate limiting is the clearest case: Stripe’s own docs note that a 429 can produce a different result under the same key, because the rate limiter runs ahead of the idempotency layer.

Reap stale in-flight rows. A process that dies mid-request leaves a key stuck in in_flight forever, and that key will reject every retry until someone notices. Give in-flight records a lease with a timeout. Store a fingerprint of the request. Hash the relevant parameters.

And the subtle one: results are only saved after execution of the endpoint begins. If the request fails validation, or conflicts with another request executing concurrently, no idempotent result is stored, and the client may retry.

The spec is blunt about retries: a client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a non-idempotent method, and a proxy MUST NOT. Everyone does it anyway, which is the whole problem. Idempotency-Key is a de-facto standard, not a standard: the IETF draft has expired without becoming an RFC, so behaviour is defined by whoever implemented it. Stripe stores the status code and body of the first request per key — including 500s — and replays that exact result, but deliberately does not store results for requests that failed validation or raced another request.

web.title: Advanced error handling | Stripe Documentation
web.description: Advanced guide for handling HTTP-level errors, idempotency, and retry logic in Stripe API integrations.
snippets: For a POST operation using an idempotency key, Stripe caches the result after the API method begins execution, including errors. Retrying a cached 400 response with the same key returns the same error. Errors that occur before execution begins, such as invalid parameters, an invalid API key, or rate limiting, don’t cache a result. Retry these requests after resolving the error.

When retrying the same operation, preserve the idempotency key and parameters within the retry window. If a 409 indicates that another request with the same key is still executing, wait and retry with that key and the same parameters.

When a connection fails, you might not know whether Stripe received or executed the request. Retry with the same idempotency key and parameters within the first 24 hours after the original request. If you still haven’t received a result when that window ends, stop retrying and reconcile the outcome as described in POST requests.

Sending the same idempotency key with different parameters produces an error indicating that the request didn’t match the original. Stripe SDKs can generate idempotency keys and retry requests automatically. Retry defaults depend on the SDK, version, and how you construct the client.

For API v1, Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request made with a given idempotency key after endpoint execution begins. Retries with the same key return the saved response, including 500 errors. With API v2, retries don’t repeat successful operations.

Stripe retries failed or partially failed work to completion when possible and returns an updated response. If a retry can’t succeed, Stripe returns an error explaining why. A client generates an idempotency key, which is a unique key that the server uses to recognize subsequent retries of the same request.
The API supports idempotency for safely retrying requests without accidentally performing the same operation twice. When creating or updating an object, use an idempotency key.

Learn how to manage the lifecycle of webhook events, including marking them as processed, understanding retry logic, and retrieving missed events.

You can mark your webhook events as processed in bulk or individually. ... Return HTTP 200 Consider all received events in the payload as successfully processed. ... Return HTTP 202 Apply specific requirements to individual orders. In the response body, list the ID number of the event you processed.

When a webhook event is not marked as processed, FastSpring automatically retries delivery for up to 7 days from the original attempt. This pattern typically results in up to 6 retries within the first 24 hours. After the first 24 hours, the system schedules 1 retry per day, for a maximum of 12 retries within the 7-day window. If the event is not processed within 7 days from the original attempt, FastSpring stops retrying and marks the event as permanently failed.

Go to Developer Tools > Webhooks > Log. Resend it manually from the order’s details page. Resend it manually from the subscription’s details page. Make a GET call to the /events/unprocessed endpoint. In both stripe-webhook and paypal-webhook, an event whose webhook_events row has processed = false is processed again on redelivery, not acknowledged. An event whose row has processed = true still returns 200 "Event already processed" without re-running the handler. On a handler error the row keeps processed = false, gets processing_attempts incremented and a non-empty processing_error, and the response is 500.

Manually verified with the Stripe CLI against a non-production project: force one handler failure (see the manual check in the prompt), confirm the 500, remove the cause, redeliver the event with stripe events resend , and confirm a payment_results row appears. Context: TortoiseWolfe/RescueDogs issue #348 — https://github.com/TortoiseWolfe/RescueDogs/issues/348 Goal: a webhook event is only "already processed" when processed = true. Failed attempts must be reprocessed on provider retry. Stripe's `incomplete` status must never be written. No schema change (webhook_events already has processing_attempts / processing_error / last_retry_at).

Then run `ALTER TABLE payment_results DROP CONSTRAINT tmp_force_fail;` and `stripe events resend `, and confirm a 200, processed=true, and exactly one new payment_results row.
